items.feedback:
- Wrong.
- You picked the option that drops the student, which is how INNER JOIN behaves. It's an easy mix-up since both joins keep matched rows.
- LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table (students). The unmatched student still shows up, with NULL in the enrollment columns.
- Review: LEFT JOIN with unmatched rows

- Correct.
- Only the 3 matched students survive an INNER JOIN.

- Partly right.
- Your core idea is right: INNER JOIN keeps only matched students, LEFT JOIN also keeps the unmatched ones.
- You said the enrollment columns come back blank rather than NULL. If a student has no enrollment row at all, what value is there to show in enrollment_id? An empty string is still a value; NULL means no value. A missing match gives NULL.
- Review: NULL vs empty string in unmatched LEFT JOIN columns

summary: 1 correct, 1 partial, 1 wrong. You can predict INNER JOIN row counts and explain the INNER vs LEFT difference in words. Work on one thing: LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched rows, filling the right-side columns with NULL. Next, write a 4-student, 3-enrollment table and predict the LEFT JOIN result row by row before running it.
